epithet.en: French observer who traveled America in 1831
epithet.da: Fransk iagttager der rejste i Amerika i 1831

1.modern-en: Tocqueville opens by declaring that equality of conditions was the single most striking fact he encountered in America, and that it shapes laws, public opinion, and the habits of the whole society. He frames his book as a warning and guide for Europe, which he believes is moving toward democracy whether it wills it or not.

21.modern-en: In his preface to Volume Two, Tocqueville explains that he set aside political institutions to focus on the deeper influence of equality on ideas, feelings, and manners. He cautions readers that he is analyzing tendencies, not predicting certainties, and that his aim is to educate rather than to flatter or denounce democracy.

96.modern-en: Tocqueville closes the entire work by reflecting on what equality has cost and what it has given humanity. He argues that equality is neither good nor bad in itself — what matters is whether democracies can preserve liberty alongside it — and ends with a call for moral and political courage in the democratic age.

epithet.en: First President and architect of American foreign policy
epithet.da: Første præsident og arkitekt bag amerikansk udenrigspolitik

9.modern-en: Tocqueville notes that Washington was among the fifty-five members of the Constitutional Convention — a gathering of exceptional talent — and credits him as the guiding presence behind the new constitution's framing.

14.modern-en: Tocqueville cites Washington's Farewell Address at length as the defining statement of American foreign policy: commercial relations with all nations, political entanglement with none. He calls it Washington's 'political bequest' to the country — a doctrine Jefferson then consolidated and that America still follows.

19.modern-en: Tocqueville quotes Washington telling Congress that Americans are 'more enlightened and more powerful than the Indian nations' and therefore bound to treat them with generosity — a principle Tocqueville notes has been systematically betrayed by settler rapacity and government tyranny toward tribes like the Cherokees.

epithet.en: The greatest Democrat America has yet produced, in Tocqueville's estimation
epithet.da: Den største demokrat Amerika hidtil har frembragt, ifølge Tocqueville

9.modern-en: Jefferson is quoted speaking on the eve of his retirement, expressing indifference to personal power — an example Tocqueville uses to illustrate how presidential character can shape the office's dignity.

11.modern-en: Tocqueville describes how Jefferson led the Republican party against the Federalists, accelerating the trend toward broader popular sovereignty and signaling the definitive triumph of democratic principles in American politics.

14.modern-en: Jefferson is cited alongside Washington as the co-architect of American foreign policy isolationism, and is also quoted lamenting the instability of American laws — evidence Tocqueville uses that even the greatest Democrat saw dangers in unchecked democratic legislating.

16.modern-en: Tocqueville quotes Jefferson warning Madison that the real tyranny to fear is legislative, not executive — a judgment Tocqueville calls the most valuable on the subject precisely because it comes from democracy's most passionate champion, not its critic.

19.modern-en: Jefferson is cited for his detailed observations on the Iroquois and for his correspondence with Lafayette about how four Eastern States were barely attached to the Union during the War of 1812 — used by Tocqueville to analyze the fragility of federal bonds and the plight of Native peoples.

epithet.en: President whose populist power revealed democracy's hidden strengths and dangers
epithet.da: Præsident hvis populistiske magt afslørede demokratiets skjulte styrker og farer

9.modern-en: Tocqueville notes that Jackson, unlike his predecessor Quincy Adams, dismissed virtually every removable federal officeholder upon taking office — illustrating how presidential patronage had become an instrument of political loyalty rather than administrative merit.

19.modern-en: Tocqueville devotes extended analysis to Jackson, whom he sees as a genuinely new kind of executive — energetic, popular, and willing to use power boldly, but also constitutionally restrained and personally opposed to expanding federal authority. He argues Jackson is less a despot than a mirror of majority will, and considers his presidency one of the genuine risks to Union stability because Jackson stoops to win the majority, then tramples obstacles once secure in its favor.

epithet.en: Federalist founder whose writings Tocqueville draws on to diagnose democratic dangers
epithet.da: Føderalistisk grundlægger hvis skrifter Tocqueville bruger til at diagnosticere demokratiets farer

9.modern-en: Hamilton is named as one of the principal founders of the Constitution and quoted from The Federalist defending the need for a strong executive — specifically the importance of energy in the chief magistrate as essential to good government.

14.modern-en: Hamilton and Jefferson are paired as the two opposing voices on the instability of democratic legislation; Tocqueville quotes Hamilton warning that frequent law changes undermine public respect for law itself, a problem he sees as endemic to democratic government.

16.modern-en: Hamilton is quoted from The Federalist on the necessity of protecting society from the tyranny of faction — that justice, not the will of the majority, must be the end of government. Tocqueville uses this alongside Jefferson to show that both parties' founders feared majority despotism.

epithet.en: New England founders whose fusion of religion and democracy shaped American civilization
epithet.da: New Englands grundlæggere hvis sammensmeltning af religion og demokrati formede den amerikanske civilisation

3.modern-en: Tocqueville devotes his most extended historical analysis to the Puritan settlers, arguing that Puritanism was simultaneously a religious and political doctrine — the most absolute democratic and republican theories fused with deep piety. He shows how their 1620 compact was the first genuine act of self-government, and argues that the seeds of both American democracy and American character were planted on the barren New England coast.

18.modern-en: Tocqueville credits Puritan New England — alongside Jesuit Canada — as one of the two great civilizing efforts among Native peoples, though he notes that neither succeeded in producing lasting integration.

19.modern-en: The Puritans appear as a contrasting backdrop to the story of the Indian tribes: the energy and self-governing traditions the Puritans brought with them are precisely what the dispossessed Native peoples lacked — and what made the European conquest so devastating and irreversible.

epithet.en: The first inhabitants, destroyed by European civilization's advance
epithet.da: De første indbyggere, ødelagt af den europæiske civilisations fremmarch

2.modern-en: Tocqueville draws on Jefferson's observations of the Iroquois to illustrate the fierce independence and stoicism of Native peoples — noting that there is no recorded instance of a captured warrior begging for his life. He frames this as evidence of a distinct civilization with its own virtues, not mere savagery.

19.modern-en: Chapter 18 is Tocqueville's fullest treatment of the 'three races.' He traces in meticulous and mournful detail how European expansion has driven Native peoples westward — not through open conquest alone, but through the advance of settlement itself, which destroys the game they live by. He singles out the Cherokees as the most tragic case: a nation that created written language, built a constitutional government, and started a newspaper — only to be forcibly expelled by state governments acting against federal law and presidential warnings. Tocqueville is unsparing: he calls the dispossession legal in form, iniquitous in fact.

20.modern-en: In the Conclusion, Tocqueville briefly revisits the vanishing of the Native nations as one of the defining facts of the American continent — a civilizational transformation whose scale and speed have no historical parallel.

epithet.en: The race whose bondage Tocqueville saw as democracy's most dangerous contradiction
epithet.da: Det folk hvis slaveri Tocqueville så som demokratiets farligste modsigelse

3.modern-en: Tocqueville notes that slavery was introduced into Virginia in 1619 — just a year before the Mayflower landing — and identifies it as the circumstance that has exercised the most profound and lasting influence on the character of Southern society, setting it apart from the democratic energies of the North.

19.modern-en: Tocqueville's most sustained and harrowing analysis: he argues that slavery has robbed Black Americans not merely of freedom but of memory, family, culture, and the very desire for liberty. He contends that prejudice — not legal slavery — is the true chain, and that it grows stronger in the North where legal slavery does not exist. He foresees either violent conflict or two permanently separate peoples sharing one republic, and judges both futures terrible. He doubts the possibility of peaceful racial integration, but also condemns slavery as incompatible with democracy's fundamental principles.

epithet.en: Constitution-framer and author of The Federalist's arguments on federal power
epithet.da: Grundlovsfader og forfatter til Federalistens argumenter om føderal magt

9.modern-en: Madison is named alongside Washington and Hamilton as one of the choicest talents in the Constitutional Convention. Tocqueville also quotes Madison's Federalist No. 45 on the division of power between Union and States — few and defined federal powers versus the numerous and indefinite powers reserved to the States.

14.modern-en: Jefferson's letter to Madison lamenting the instability of American laws is cited by Tocqueville as evidence that even the architects of the republic recognized the democratic tendency toward legislative restlessness as a serious defect.

epithet.en: President whose loss to Jackson illustrated the democratic spoils system at work
epithet.da: Præsident hvis tab til Jackson illustrerede demokratiets byttehandel-system i praksis

9.modern-en: Tocqueville uses Adams as a case study in presidential patronage: on entering office, Adams dismissed the majority of those appointed by his predecessor, and Jackson in turn dismissed virtually all of Adams's appointees — illustrating how democratic elections destabilize the entire administrative apparatus of government.

epithet.en: Chief Justice whose biography of Washington illuminates the republic's founding struggles
epithet.da: Højesteretspræsident hvis biografi om Washington belyser republikkens grundlæggende kampe

3.modern-en: Tocqueville cites Marshall's Life of Washington for historical data on the early Virginia settlements and the character of the first colonists — using the biography as a primary source for his account of the Anglo-American origins.

14.modern-en: Marshall's account of Washington's presidency is quoted to illustrate how even the most respected leader cannot for long resist the torrent of popular opinion — a vivid example of the limits that democratic majorities place on executive independence in foreign policy.
